By default we have

example : 1 - 2 = 0 := by rfl

is there a way to change this default behavior that by default elaborates numbers as Nat? I would like to elaborate number as Int.
RFL does it already
RFL ?

Ahh I think I didn't write the question correctly. I'm more interested in figuring out how to change Lean such that 

example : 1 - 2 = -1 := by <what-ever tactic>

It is about what does 1 - 2 elaborates to. Not about the proof.
make an instance HSub Nat Nat Int with higher priority?
example : 1 - 2 = -1 := by rfl? It gives you an Integer.
Let me share the link: https://live.lean-lang.org/#codez=KYDwhgtgDgNsAEAueBGeBaeAmeBeDai%2BARgJ7wBOAZjEA

I would like to quote Bjarne Stroustrup here:

I see two primary arguments for using unsigned subscripts and sizes:
• That’s what we have been doing since the adoption of the STL in 1996.
• Sizes cannot be negative
and two primary reasons for using signed subscripts and sizes:
• Signed values are the result of most integer calculations
• In C and C++, unsigned does not model natural numbers

I will dig into the arguments and consider alternatives, but my conclusion stands:
Use signed subscripts and sizes for span as it was deliberately designed to do. The original use of unsigned for the STL was a bad mistake and should be corrected (eventually).

I should have the choice to have Int as the canonical number type.
I'm not sure about the point of mentioning Stepanov's STL and Lean here, can you explain?
It is about API design and the question is about what does 1 - 2 elaborates to by default.

If you were to override this instance as the default one https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Init/Prelude.html#instOfNatNat it should work. But I would very much recommend against doing that as it can cause unforseen effects, e.g. when working with macros that produce numeric literals
(deleted)

I see, yeah I was a bit worried that changing this behavior would have bad consequences as the rest of Lean was not designed for it.

My question is maybe XY problem. What I'm working on matrix/tensor API and I'm debating whether to use Nat or Int. If Nat then I'm forced to use Int anyway if I want to do any more complicated arithmetic. If using Int then I stay in one type territory.
What's stopping you from just using Int though? If type inference can figure out that Int was intended Int will be chosen

Well my concern it what do I get when I write (-4,5)...(3,10)? Right now I get Std.Rco (ℤ × ℕ) so in the loop

for i in (-4,5)...(3,10) do
   s += A[offset + i]

probably offset is of type ℕ × ℕ. Then I probably have HAdd (ℕ × ℕ) (ℤ × ℕ) (ℤ × ℕ) so now I need to to make sure that A has GetElem Matrix (ℕ × ℕ) _ _, GetElem Matrix (ℤ × ℕ) _ _, GetElem Matrix (ℕ × ℤ) _ _, GetElem Matrix (ℤ × ℤ) _ _. Which is doable, I'm just debating if this is the right approach.

Alternative is to force everything to be Int and that is why I'm asking this question.

Nice, it works

@[implicit_reducible, default_instance 200]
instance instOfNatNat' (n : Nat) : OfNat ℤ n := ⟨n⟩

-- 10 : ℤ
#check 10

-- (-4, 5)...(3, 10) : Std.Rco (ℤ × ℤ)
#check (-4,5)...(3,10)

but yeah debatable if a good idea to put this at the top of my project ...

  • 5
  • · + ·
  • ·[·]

This question is effectively asking, can I place the burden on 5? Right now, I don't know what is the best option so I'm exploring all.

Wow, is this really the behavior that we want? 

example : 1 - 2 = 0 := by rfl -- passes

example : 1 - 2 = -1 := by rfl -- passes

I do appreciate that Lean is able to automatically infer that we're dealing with Nat in the first instance and Int in the second, without forcing the coercion, but ... ???
This is why formal-conjectures has the answer() elaborator, because it makes 1 - 2 = answer(-1) illegal

Not a solution to the original problem but if the problem is that (2 : Int) is clunky to type, then maybe you could have notation like 2z or 2Z or 2i (admittedly, this last one looks like a complex number) which forces 2 to be an integer. I think Java has stuff like 1000L and 1.3F, and Rust has something similar like 1u32. I can't remember if Lean has something similar.

I recommend 1n, 1z, 1q, 1r, 1c, 1u32, 1u64, 1usize, 1i32, 1i64, and 1isize for (1 : Nat), (1 : Int), (1 : Rat), (1 : Real), (1 : Complex), (1 : UInt32), (1 : USize), (1 : Int32), (1 : Int64), and (1 : ISize) (we should mostly copy rust notation on the fixed size ones). Unsure what the notation should be for Float and Float32. 1i should be invalid notation to avoid looking like an imaginary number. Also 1c for (1 : Complex) might look weird when you mix it with Complex.I
That standard literal in C for Float is 1.0d and for Float32 is 1.0f
That's true, but my thought was that maybe anything with a number after it took a fixed number of bytes and everything else was unbounded, so 1.0f32 for Float32 and 1.0f64 for Float
Also what would the notation be if we ever implemented complex floating point numbers? 1c32 and 1c64?
Can’t we change the default OfNat instance so that + defaults to expecting Nat, while - defaults to expecting Int?

Or use ∸ to denote - on Nat.
After all, denoting monus as minus isn't consistent with the embedding of Nat into Int.
And of course ⫽ for "div"

Actually Nat.monus is more mathematically analogous to Set.sdiff than Int.sub.
So we could have 1 \ 2 = 0 instead of 1 - 2 = 0.
